definitions.definition: What exists by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and is not further reducible: consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbāna, in contrast to concepts (paññatti).
Conventional truth: persons, beings, chariots and the like, designated on the basis of ultimate dhammas; true by common usage but not found on analysis.
In the forest teachers' usage, the conventions of the world (names, selves, even the Dhamma's words) which the released heart still uses but is no longer bound by; contrasted with vimutti.

A concept or designation: either the concept as meaning, which is made known (e.g. 'person', 'direction', a kasiṇa sign), or the concept as name, which makes it known; it lacks intrinsic nature and is not an ultimate reality.
The particular nature by which a dhamma is what it is (e.g. hardness for the earth element); dhammas are defined as bearing their own intrinsic nature.
In the Abhidhamma, an elementary constituent of experience that bears its own nature; the matrices classify all dhammas, conditioned and unconditioned.
The schedule of triads and dyads at the head of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (and the lists heading other books) by which dhammas are classified.

(1) The three characteristics impermanence, suffering and not-self; (2) in the commentaries' defining method, the characteristic of a dhamma, given together with its function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).
Consciousness, the bare knowing of an object and forerunner of the mental factors; the first ultimate reality, classified into 89 (or 121) types; synonymous with viññāṇa and mano.

The heart-mind, 'the one who knows' (Thai: phu ru): the knowing nature which the forest teachers train and purify and which, when released, is described as pure and not subject to death (Ajahn Maha Boowa).
The noting mind, observed arising and passing together with its object.
A mental factor that arises and ceases together with consciousness, has the same object and base; fifty-two are enumerated.
Matter: that which is 'molested' (ruppati) by cold, heat etc.; the third ultimate reality, twenty-eight kinds; as an object, the visible form.

The unconditioned element, the fourth ultimate reality: cessation of craving and of the round, object of the path and fruition knowledges; one in nature, twofold as with and without residue, threefold as void, signless and desireless; not a self.
Coolness: the extinction of the fires of defilement, tasted here and now, momentarily or completely (Buddhadāsa).
Taught by the Dhammakāya tradition as a realm and a true self (attā) where the Dhammakāyas of the Buddhas abide — contested by other Theravāda scholars.
The experience beyond the field of mind and matter, reached when all saṅkhāras are eradicated.

equivalents.note: the same Buddhist term in Sanskrit; the Gītā's brahma-nirvāṇa and other Hindu usages differ

definitions.definition: Not produced by conditions: in the Theravāda only nibbāna is unconditioned; the Kathāvatthu rejects the views that space, dependent origination or the truths are unconditioned.
Epithet of nibbāna: where there is no death.
Wholesome: consciousness and factors rooted in non-greed, non-hatred and (often) non-delusion, blameless and producing pleasant results.
Unwholesome: consciousness rooted in greed, hatred or delusion, blameworthy and producing painful results; twelve types.
Neither wholesome nor unwholesome: resultants, functionals, all matter and nibbāna.
Resultant consciousness and factors produced by past kamma; kammically indeterminate.
Consciousness that performs a function without being kamma or result — e.g. adverting, and all the impulsions of an arahant.
Consciousness without any of the six roots: the eighteen rootless types.
Consciousness or mental factors accompanied by beautiful roots; the twenty-five beautiful mental factors.
The six roots — greed, hatred, delusion and their opposites — that give stability to consciousness; also the root condition of the Paṭṭhāna.
Greed, the unwholesome root of attachment to objects; characteristic grasping.
Hatred, the unwholesome root; characteristic ferocity.
Delusion, the unwholesome root present in all unwholesome consciousness; characteristic blindness to the object's true nature; synonymous with ignorance.
Consciousness that mostly occurs in the sense-sphere planes: fifty-four types.
Consciousness of the fine-material sphere: the jhānas and their results and functionals (fifteen types).
Consciousness of the four formless attainments (twelve types).
Transcending the world of the five aggregates: the four paths, four fruits and nibbāna.
Contact: the coming together of object, sense faculty and consciousness; the first of the universal factors.
Feeling: the experiencing of the object's flavour as pleasant, painful or neutral (bodily or mental); a universal mental factor and an aggregate.
Bodily sensation, observed objectively as the meeting-point of mind and matter; reaction to it with craving or aversion generates saṅkhāras (Goenka).
Perception: the noting and recognizing of an object's marks; a universal mental factor and an aggregate.
Volition: the factor that organizes its associates in acting on the object; it is kamma (the Buddha: 'volition is kamma').
Unification of mind on its object; a universal factor, developed as concentration and the jhāna factor.

equivalents.note: Yoga uses ekāgratā for a level of mind; the Abhidhamma makes it a factor present in every consciousness

definitions.definition: Attention: the turning of the mind to the object; a universal factor.
The faculty that sustains its co-arising dhammas; mental (a universal factor) and material (in kamma-born matter).
Applied thought: the mounting of the mind onto the object; a factor of the first jhāna.

equivalents.note: cf. the Yoga Sūtra's savitarka samādhi

definitions.definition: Sustained thought: continued pressure of the mind on the object; a factor of the first jhāna (and of the second in the fivefold scheme).
Decision about the object; an occasional factor; as an imperfection of insight, strong resolve (faith).
Energy, effort; occasional factor, faculty, power and awakening factor.
Rapture: delight in the object; fivefold (minor, momentary, showering, uplifting, pervading); a jhāna factor.
Wish to act regarding the object; ethically variable; one of the four predominants.
Pleasant feeling; a jhāna factor, distinguished from rapture as the enjoyment is from the thirst for water.
Lack of moral shame; one of the four universal unwholesome factors.
Lack of moral dread; a universal unwholesome factor.
Agitation of mind; a universal unwholesome factor; a fetter abandoned only by arahantship.
Sceptical doubt about the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, training and conditionality; a hindrance and fetter abandoned at stream-entry.
Shame at wrongdoing, arising from self-respect; a beautiful universal.
Dread of wrongdoing, arising from regard for others and fear of consequences; a beautiful universal.
Balance, keeping the associated states even; a beautiful universal, the factor that becomes the divine abiding of equanimity.
Tranquillity of the mental body and of consciousness; beautiful universals; an awakening factor and an imperfection of insight when grasped.
Mindfulness: non-floating on the object, not forgetting it; a beautiful universal, faculty, power, awakening factor and path factor.
Bare, precise noting of whatever arises in the present moment.
Continuous awareness of sensations throughout the body with understanding of impermanence.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit smṛti also means remembrance and tradition (Dharmaśāstra); the Buddhist sense is present-moment mindfulness

definitions.definition: Confidence in the Triple Gem; beautiful universal; faculty and power; the wholesome counterpart of greed in the greedy temperament.
Understanding: insight knowledge associated with wholesome consciousness, penetrating dhammas as they are; the third training.

equivalents.note: the same Buddhist term; Hindu usages of prajñā differ

definitions.definition: Mental factors not named in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī's lists but included by its phrase 'or whatever other states there are', identified by the commentaries (e.g. desire, decision, attention, balance).
The four primary elements — earth (hardness), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion/support) — on which all derived matter depends.
The twenty-four kinds of matter dependent on the great elements.

The material base of the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, identified by the commentaries as the heart; the Paṭṭhāna speaks only of 'the matter in dependence on which' they occur, and the Dhammasaṅgaṇī does not list it.
The smallest units of matter: groups of inseparable elements (at least eight) arising and ceasing together.
Tiny particles seen with the light of access or jhāna concentration and analysed into their elements as the basis of insight.
The subtle units whose rapid arising and passing is experienced as vibration in the body (U Ba Khin).
Temperature (the fire element) as one of the four originators of matter.
Nutritive essence, present in every material group; nutriment as an originator of matter.
A cognitive series of mind-moments in fixed order through a door, e.g. seventeen moments for a very great object at a sense door.

The resultant consciousness that maintains the continuity of an existence when no active process occurs; the same type as the rebirth-linking and death consciousness; identified by the commentary with the 'luminous mind'.
The active phase of a cognitive process, normally seven moments, where wholesome or unwholesome kamma is made (functional in arahants).
Two resultant moments that may follow the impulsions in a sense-sphere process, taking the same object.
The object of consciousness; six kinds; object condition in the Paṭṭhāna.
The physical base of consciousness: the five sense organs and the heart-base.
Rebirth-linking consciousness, the first moment of a new existence, conditioned by the last process of the previous one.
The last consciousness of an existence, of the same type as its life-continuum.
An object connected with a past deed (e.g. a weapon, an offering) presenting itself to the mind of the dying.
A sign of the coming destination (hell-fire, a womb, celestial mansions) presenting itself to the dying.
Volition (cetanā) and the wholesome or unwholesome action it motivates; kamma condition for results and kamma-born matter; classified by function, weight, time and place.

equivalents.note: Buddhist kamma is defined as volition; Mīmāṃsā and Jain uses of karma differ (ritual act; subtle matter)

definitions.definition: Kamma that ripens with priority: the five heinous crimes, fixed wrong view, or the jhānas.
A plane of existence (thirty-one) or of consciousness (four).
The four woeful planes: hell, animal realm, ghosts, asuras.
An existence between death and rebirth — rejected by the Theravāda (Kathāvatthu 8.2), which holds that rebirth-linking follows death immediately.
A world-age with four incalculable phases (contraction, contracted, expansion, expanded).
The beginningless round of rebirths, which has no maker or experiencer but only dhammas occurring by conditions.
The three rounds of dependent origination: of defilement, of kamma and of result.
That which is helpful to the arising or persistence of another dhamma; the Paṭṭhāna enumerates twenty-four modes.
Explanation of conditionality through the twenty-four conditions, as opposed to the dependent-origination method.
Strong-dependence condition: earlier states, persons, climate, food and lodging as powerful supports for later states.
Support condition: a dhamma as foundation of another, e.g. the physical bases for consciousness.

The twelve-linked arising of suffering from ignorance; expounded by the commentaries across three lives (three periods, twenty modes, four groups, three links), and by the Abhidhamma method within one moment.
The arising of suffering and of the 'I' in the present, from contact without mindfulness; 'birth' is the birth of the ego (Buddhadāsa).
The chart of dependent origination to be understood before contemplating the arising and passing of mind and feeling.
Not knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation and the way; the first link.

equivalents.note: Advaita's avidyā is a cosmic superimposition; the Abhidhamma's avijjā is a mental factor (delusion)

definitions.definition: (1) The second link: meritorious, demeritorious and imperturbable volitions; (2) the aggregate of mental formations (fifty mental factors); (3) all conditioned things.
Mental reactions of craving and aversion to sensations, and the deep conditioning they leave, which arise as sensations when observed with equanimity (Goenka).

equivalents.note: Yoga's saṃskāra is a latent impression; the Pali term is wider

definitions.definition: The mental aggregates (or feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention) and matter; in insight, defined as all there is in place of a being.
Craving for sense pleasures, existence and non-existence; the origin of suffering; analysed into 108 modes.
Clinging: to sense pleasures, views, rules and observances, and a doctrine of self.
The five aggregates: matter, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness.
The twelve bases (six internal, six external); also the formless 'spheres'.
The eighteen elements (six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses); the four great elements; nibbāna as the unconditioned element.
The twenty-two faculties, including the sense faculties, life, the feelings, the five spiritual faculties and the three supramundane faculties.
A person: a conventional designation (paññatti), not an ultimate reality; the Puggalapaññatti classifies persons, and the Kathāvatthu refutes the view that the person is a real and ultimate fact.
Taints: of sensual desire, existence, views and ignorance (four in the Abhidhamma).

Fetters binding to the round; the Abhidhamma lists ten (sensual lust, aversion, conceit, view, doubt, rules and observances, lust for existence, envy, avarice, ignorance), differing from the sutta list.
Hindrances obstructing concentration and insight; six in the Abhidhamma (the sutta five plus ignorance).
The ten bases of defilement: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing.

equivalents.note: Yoga's five kleśas and the Abhidhamma's ten overlap partly

definitions.definition: Seven latent tendencies lying dormant in the continuum until conditions arouse them.
Four bodily ties: covetousness, ill will, clinging to rules, dogmatic insistence 'this alone is true'.
Wrong view grasping beyond the true nature of things.
View; as an unwholesome factor, wrong view, especially of self and of the world.
Conceit: measuring oneself as better, equal or worse; a fetter abandoned only by arahantship.
A meditation subject (forty in the Visuddhimagga), given by a teacher; also meditation practice generally.
In Thai usage 'kammathan' names meditation practice and the forest monks devoted to it (phra kammathan).
The old meditation system itself (kammaṭṭhāna borān).
A device (disk of earth, water, fire, colour, light, space) used to produce the learning and counterpart signs and the jhānas; ten are listed.
The ten kinds of corpse as meditation subjects, and the perception of the body's foulness, counteracting lust.
The ten recollections among the forty subjects.
Recollection of death, by simple attention or in eight ways; it leads to access.
In the Visuddhimagga, the contemplation of the thirty-two parts as repulsive, leading to the first jhāna.
Mindfulness of in- and out-breathing in sixteen bases, worked by counting, following, contact, fixing and the later stages; leads to all four jhānas and, with insight, to arahantship.
The complete practice in four tetrads covering all four foundations of mindfulness (Buddhadāsa).
Awareness of natural respiration at the entrance of the nostrils, the first days of a course.
Loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity developed towards all beings without limit; each has a near and a far enemy.
Wishing welfare to beings; developed first towards oneself and then, with the barriers broken down, to all.

equivalents.note: YS 1.33 cultivates maitrī towards the happy; the Visuddhimagga's mettā is a meditation subject leading to jhāna

definitions.definition: The point in loving-kindness at which one's mind is equal towards self, dear, neutral and hostile persons; sign and access arise.
The four formless attainments beyond the fine-material jhānas.
Imperturbability, said of the fourth jhāna and formless attainments.
Meditative absorption with specific factors; fourfold in the suttas and fivefold in the Abhidhamma method; mundane or supramundane.
Full absorption on a counterpart sign in which the mind is unbroken for long periods; required (or access) before seeing ultimate realities.

equivalents.note: Yoga's dhyāna is the seventh limb, a flow of cognition; Buddhist jhāna is a graded absorption with factors

definitions.definition: Wholesome one-pointedness of mind, placing consciousness and concomitants evenly on one object; threefold as momentary, access and absorption.
Concentration in the neighbourhood of absorption, with the hindrances suppressed and the counterpart sign present.
Full absorption (jhāna), following access.
Concentration lasting only for the moment, named in the Visuddhimagga among the three kinds; in the sub-commentary, the unification of mind of the pure-insight practitioner.
Concentration arising from uninterrupted moment-to-moment noting, strong enough to suppress the hindrances and support insight without prior jhāna.
A mental image or sign: preliminary, learning and counterpart signs; also the 'signs' of formations transcended by the signless.
The light and the breath-sign that appear with deep concentration and must stabilize before jhāna.
Visions and signs arising in meditation, to be investigated and not clung to.
The mental image of the object perceived as clearly with eyes closed as with eyes open, still showing the device's faults.
A purified, stable image born of perception, free of the device's faults, appearing with access concentration; for the breath it may appear as a star, gem, cotton, smoke, cloud and so on.
The five masteries of a jhāna: adverting, attaining, resolving, emerging, reviewing.
The ten impediments to be cut before meditation: dwelling, family, gain, following, building work, travel, kin, affliction, books, supernormal powers.
The teacher who gives the meditation subject, endowed with the seven qualities; the Buddha is the best good friend.
The six temperaments — greedy, hating, deluded, faithful, intelligent, speculative — determining suitable meditation subjects.
The thirteen ascetic practices allowed by the Buddha for effacement and contentment.
The austerities central to forest practice: alms-food only, one meal, forest and charnel-ground dwelling, refuse-rag robes, wandering (tudong).
Virtue: volition, concomitants, restraint and non-transgression; fourfold purity for monks.
The monastic code; restraint by it is the first of the four purities of virtue.
Guarding the sense doors so that covetousness and grief do not invade; the second purity of virtue.
Livelihood; its purity is the third purity of virtue, violated by scheming, talking, hinting, belittling and seeking gain with gain.
Supernormal power, tenfold (by resolve, transformation, mind-made, etc.); the worldling's power is fragile and an impediment to insight.

equivalents.note: the Yoga and haṭha siddhis are comparable attainments; the Visuddhimagga's warnings parallel YS 3.37

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma; a mundane direct knowledge.
Direct knowledge recollecting former existences; its range differs among sectarians, disciples, paccekabuddhas and Buddhas.
Insight into the three characteristics of formations, developed through the purifications and insight knowledges.
Continuous noting of all arising mental and physical phenomena, through which the insight knowledges unfold.
Observing bodily sensations systematically and with equanimity, understanding their impermanence (the Goenka course).
Seeing the emptiness of 'I' and 'mine' in the midst of daily life.
Tranquillity of mind through concentration on one of the forty subjects.
One who develops jhāna first and then insight, discerning mentality through the jhāna factors.

literal: one whose vehicle is pure insight

definitions.definition: One who develops insight without prior jhāna, beginning with the four elements.
One whose insight is 'dry', not moistened by jhāna; his path has first-jhāna character; he does not attain cessation.
Purity; nibbāna; the seven purifications that make up the path.
Three full understandings: as the known, as investigation, as abandoning.
Ten experiences that arise with tender insight (illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquillity, bliss, resolution, exertion, assurance, equanimity, attachment) and are mistaken for the path.
Light arising from insight; the first imperfection of insight.
Subtle attachment to insight experiences — both an imperfection and a basis of imperfection.

literal: knowledge of contemplating rise and fall

definitions.definition: Insight seeing the arising and passing of formations; in its tender form beset by the imperfections.
Insight seeing only the dissolution of formations, with eight benefits.
Insight that looks on formations with equanimity, neither fearing nor delighting; the peak of mundane insight.
The last mundane insight, conforming to the eight preceding knowledges and to the requisites of awakening.
The moment that takes nibbāna as object and passes from the worldling's lineage to the noble lineage (also, before a jhāna, from the sense sphere to the exalted).
The supramundane path consciousness, occurring once for each of the four stages, which abandons the corresponding fetters.
The fruition consciousness following the path, and re-entered as fruition attainment.
Reviewing knowledge after path and fruit: nineteen kinds in all.
Abandoning of defilements by substitution of opposites, suppression, cutting off, tranquillization and escape.
Signless: the gateway of liberation through contemplation of impermanence; an aspect of nibbāna.
Desireless: the gateway through contemplation of suffering.
Voidness: all dhammas void of self; the gateway through contemplation of not-self; an aspect of nibbāna.
The mind void of 'I' and 'mine' — the heart of Buddhism, to be lived in daily work (Buddhadāsa).
Not-self: no dhamma, conditioned or unconditioned, is a self; there is suffering but no sufferer.
Suspension of consciousness and mental factors, attained only by non-returners and arahants with the eight attainments.
One who has reached the purification by overcoming doubt and is sure of a good destiny.

literal: things on the side of awakening

definitions.definition: The thirty-seven requisites of awakening; all are present in the path moment.
One who has destroyed the taints; the Kathāvatthu denies that an arahant can fall away, have ignorance or doubt, be defiled by deities, or remain a householder.
A noble person still in training (the first seven noble persons).
The arahant.
An ordinary person who has not reached a path.
One who touches the eight liberations with the body and whose taints are destroyed by wisdom.
One whose taints are destroyed by wisdom without having touched the eight liberations.
Liberation of mind; in Thai forest usage the released heart beyond conventions.
The state of the heart when all defilements are gone, contrasted with sammuti (convention).
Epithet of the Buddha; the Kathāvatthu rejects views that he did not really live in the human world or that Buddhas stand in all directions.
Knowledge, classified in the Vibhaṅga from one to ten kinds; the insight knowledges.
The four analytical knowledges: of meaning, Dhamma, language and ready expression.
Language; knowledge of the language of intrinsic nature (Māgadhī).
Identified by the commentaries with the Pali of the texts and called the root language of all beings, the language of intrinsic nature.
Consciousness as an aggregate and a link; synonymous with citta.
Clear comprehension, fourfold: of purpose, suitability, domain and non-delusion.
The four foundations: body, feeling, mind, dhammas; matched by the commentary to four kinds of practitioner.
Penetration of the truths; the Theravāda holds that each path penetrates all four truths at once.
The Sabbatthivāda thesis that dhammas exist in the three times, refuted in the Kathāvatthu.
Sharing or dedication of merit to others, especially the departed; the Kathāvatthu denies a literal transfer of the gift itself.
Self-designation of the Theravāda of the Mahāvihāra as 'those who analyse'.
The mind called luminous in AN 1.49–52, identified by the commentary with the life-continuum.
The radiant citta of the forest teachers' experience; Ajahn Maha Boowa warns that ignorance hides in this radiance.
In the canon, an epithet of the Buddha as embodying the Dhamma; in the Dhammakāya tradition, the luminous Buddha-form found within the body at the seventh base.
The inner Buddha-body reached through successive refined bodies at the centre of the body.
The Thai forest parikamma word repeated with the breath ('bud-' in, '-dho' out) or alone to steady the mind; also a recollection of the Buddha.
Preparatory repetition that leads the citta to converge; Ajahn Mun's and Ajahn Lee's basic instruction.
Wandering ascetic practice in forests and mountains, with alms-round, umbrella-tent (klot) and forest dwelling.
The wandering forest life of the kammaṭṭhāna monks.
Buddhadāsa's term for a mind void of 'I' and 'mine', with which one should work and live.
The mind free of self-grasping, the practical form of suññatā.
The recitation used in Dhammakāya meditation while visualizing a crystal sphere at the centre of the body.
The parikamma mantra of the Dhammakāya method.
The Buddha's dispensation, expected to decline through five disappearances; the urgency of practice within it was stressed by Ledi Sayadaw and U Ba Khin.
The perfections fulfilled by a Bodhisatta (ten in the Theravāda list), treated systematically in Dhammapāla's commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka.
Impermanence, the first characteristic; in insight, seen as the rise and fall of formations.
Experienced directly as the arising and passing of sensations throughout the body (U Ba Khin: 'anicca' as the key).
The second characteristic and first truth; 'there is suffering but no one who suffers'.
Pleasant feeling, where the latent tendency to sensual lust lies.
